SYSTEMIC ADVENTURE ENGINE — FROM CURIOSITY TO LEGEND

Irreverents • Vision-level mechanics proposal • 22 November 2026

# The single-game premise

Exploration, stealth, combat, pursuit, ability puzzles, vehicles and Hall recognition are not separate minigames. They are different ways of interacting with the same world: player actions change objects and inhabitants; those reactions change the situation; players improvise; extraordinary outcomes may become legends.

The goal is a reusable, understandable set of rules that produces multiple valid solutions and delightful accidents.

# The adventure loop

Observe a peculiar thing → wonder what might happen → choose character/power → interact (silently, forcefully, socially or foolishly) → the world reacts → the player escalates, solves, sneaks, fights or escapes → world and NPCs remember → discover new possibility or route → perhaps the Hall notices.

At any point the party can abandon its original objective. This is central to the anti-story experience.

# Five shared physical affordance families

ACCESS: fitting through, flying over, unlocking, disguising, tunneling or opening.

FORCE: lifting, holding, throwing, slamming, pushing, colliding and destroying.

ENERGY: heating, cooling, igniting, charging, blowing, redirecting and sustaining.

INFORMATION: seeing, hearing, talking to animals, deciphering, distracting, remembering and tracking.

PRESENCE: being seen or unseen, attracting attention, influencing NPCs, recruiting help or provoking resistance.

A level designer can express an obstacle as combinations of these properties. Avoid a door that just says “green character required” unless the fiction supports a unique identity/permission.

# World-object behavior language

Candidate object attributes: material, mass band, break threshold, state, movable/anchored, conductive, flammable, wet, freezing, obstructive, loudness on impact, social ownership and security importance.

Examples:

An unattended chest can be opened quietly; a weak wall can be smashed; a gate can be held with a strong character or propped by a movable object; a water valve alters level routes; a mechanical defender can be hijacked; a fragile jewel display triggers suspicion if broken.

These are high-level targets. Don't imply a full physics engine that simulates everything with real materials. Choose the most expressive interactions and make them reliable everywhere they're advertised.

# A puzzle should be a situation, not a prescribed password

Example: two pressure plates must remain pressed to raise a gate. In co-op, two people do so simultaneously. Solo player may move a crate onto one plate, freeze a lever in place, or trick an enemy into standing there. No code checks human player count.

Example: a hanging object guards a passage; use cutting, force, wind, flight, a moving vehicle, or enemy collision as different pathways when world rules permit.

Example: a living creature blocks a tunnel; talk, lure, scare, sneak past, defeat or change the environment. Do not require every solution to exist everywhere, only that outcomes arise honestly from established systems.

# Alert mechanics across the whole world

An NPC may see trespass, hear an impact, notice a stolen object, hear a witness or observe violence. Suspicion rises based on evidence. Investigators search last-known positions and call help when danger or proof warrants it.

Alarms are persistent local world events, not menu states. Reinforcements can enter through doors, streets, shafts or vehicle routes. Response intensity grows with duration, threat severity, damage, public danger and successful resistance by heroes.

Escalation should unlock more interesting foes and tools. New defenders may carry copyable powers, shields, machines and vehicles.

# Three excellent outcomes for one mission

SILENT MASTERY: enter, interact, take, leave. No alarm. Feel clever and competent.

GLORIOUS DEFIANCE: become surrounded, resist far beyond reasonable expectations, create spectacular chain impacts. Loss can still be noteworthy.

IMPOSSIBLE ESCAPE: break pursuit through ingenious movement, vehicle hijack, stealth disappearance or a last-second environmental interaction. Narrow survival is thrilling.

This triple outcome is owner-confirmed. The same level space should support all three.

# Impact as a world event

Anticipation makes force legible; hit-stop/impact frame makes contact readable; launch, wall impact, debris and enemy-to-enemy collision express consequences; recovery preserves flow.

When a strong hero suplexes a guard into a weak wall, the wall can crack. The noise attracts nearby guards. Their response machine can be hijacked. Its collision might uncover a hidden entrance. A player should recognize one connected chain of events, not four unrelated scripted interactions.

# Vehicles as capability multipliers

A vehicle should be a world thing, not an isolated race screen. It has operator, direction, accessible controls, mass/speed category, impact interaction and possible hijack opportunity. A stolen machine can block a street, carry comrades, smash defenses, make noise, or become the reason a much bigger pursuit begins.

Two-dimensional driving need not imitate fully 3D GTA. What matters is side-view traversal, speed, collisions, simple usable controls and the freedom to steal a machine sent to stop you.

# Failure without exhausting fun

No mandatory hard reset when stealth goes wrong. Avoid making ordinary defeat destroy hours of progress. One possible design is safe respawn in or near a discovered region, with local repairs and lasting social consequences. This exact recovery policy is OPEN.

Failure should have risk—lost cargo, heat, alarms, temporary shutdowns or reinforcements—so a narrow escape matters. But punishing recovery time should not become the main source of difficulty.

# Hall of Legends recognition, proposed layers

1. EPISODE DETECTION: recognize infiltration attempt, extended combat, pursuit and escape; episodes can overlap.

2. HIGHLIGHT CANDIDATES: capture intense, dramatic or counterintuitive frames: a suplex, blocked road, one-HP getaway, undetected vault opening, catastrophe involving a rare machine.

3. CONTEXT: estimate security bypassed, opposition scale, duration, closeness to detection/defeat, amount of valuable loot, degree of control, how unusual the combination was.

4. HISTORICAL COMPARISON: compare to party's prior episodes in the SAME category and perhaps across historical dimensions. A zero-alarm rescue need not compete with destruction count.

5. COMMEMORATION: select representative screenshot, title, participants, location, time, contextual stats, and place artifact on Hall pedestal.

6. AFTERMATH: affected people talk about incident; Hall itself stays playable, and its own security can become target for another legend.

These steps are a design architecture, not a finalized machine-learning classifier or scoring formula.

# Relative record, not task completion checklist

“A heist of unprecedented security” and “an unbelievable last stand against 80 elite units” are incomparable on a single kill-count scale. Keep meaningful categories and relative records. Participants include people who lured enemies, supported, entered the encounter late, caused the catastrophe or were defeated. All share credit when genuinely part of event.

Not every exciting accident should generate a popup. Selectivity makes recognition surprising and valuable. A journal for lesser incidents is possible but unconfirmed.

# Example of emergent chain reaction

A cautious infiltration into a castle archive gets interrupted by the player's attempt to steal a wizard's potion.

The wizard notices, tries to stop them, and accidentally ignites a spilled substance; guards arrive.

A grappler throws one guard into a row of old shelves, revealing a crawlspace.

A friend steals the wheel controls of a suppression cart sent by the guards; the machine barrels through a barricade.

The party escapes through the revealed passage with one HP and a worthless but fascinating magical pill.

The Hall may remember the escape. The court remembers a robbery. The wizard remembers personal indignity. The player remembers a perfect afternoon.

No single cutscene is required for that story.

# Regional memory and material recovery

Environmental destruction changes momentary routes; inhabitants react, flee or mobilize. Over time, repair crews may reconstruct a bridge, a shop may close and reopen, guards may fortify a gate, and rumors persist. Keep historical memory separate from transient destruction so players do not corrupt a save merely through ordinary experimentation.

If a destroyed hallway is the only route to an essential service, the world needs a physical alternate route or repair mechanism. Do not use invisible “essential structure cannot break” rules without clear context.

# Cooperative architecture, vision level

One SHARED expedition party selected from a permanently expanding unlocked roster. Multiple online players take control of separate members; solo switches among same finite party slots. Co-op adds simultaneous activity and the possibility of the party splitting into different areas.

Do not create an arbitrary two-player human requirement when physics allows a solo workaround. Some challenges may still be impractical alone. Temporary acquired powers and roles should complement each other, not guarantee that every challenge has one assigned hero answer.

# Pacing: calm before impact

Visuals and sound should be gentle enough during normal exploration that a major collision, alarm, chase or special ability feels contrastively extraordinary. The owner specifically noted that Kirby avoids overstimulation better than recent images. A game with constant sparks, flashes, particle effects and alarms cannot deliver rare “OHHHH!” moments.

A quiet town should look and sound different from the same town under pursuit. Stealth UI should be readable but restrained.

# Content design template for every area

What is this place for when the player isn't here?

What is visually peculiar and attractive to investigate?

What can be acquired, stolen, borrowed, moved or destroyed?

What is a quiet route to an interesting goal?

What happens if someone gets caught or deliberately causes trouble?

What machinery or powerful enemies might respond?

Where can a clever party escape?

Which old mysteries become interesting when a new type/power is acquired?

Could an extraordinary incident here earn a Hall record?

What consequences would still be visible on returning?

# Biggest design risks

TOO MUCH SIMULATION: expensive, buggy interactions nobody understands. Counter: compact, consistent affordance families.

TOO MANY FORCED SOLUTIONS: static icons replace experimentation. Counter: physical constraints and emergent alternatives.

TOO LITTLE CONSEQUENCE: violent NPC reaction is a brief cosmetic animation. Counter: local pursuit, social memory and altered defenses.

TOO MUCH PUNISHMENT: failed stealth becomes reload; pursuit becomes slog. Counter: enjoyable impact and multiple escape routes.

TOO MUCH VISUAL NOISE: secrets and impacts lost amid clutter. Counter: clean backgrounds and high-contrast action.

TOO MUCH STORY PROTECTION: essential character immunity makes the game's freedom feel fraudulent. Counter: authored fallback and event-system reactions, scoped to feasibility.

TOO MANY HALL AWARDS: “legendary” loses meaning. Counter: relative records and selective recognition.

# Prototype checklist, before full production

One 2D royal-city space with two entrances to a secret vault; two or three functional character types, an acquired power, ordinary town NPCs, guards with at least two response tiers, simple hiding, one satisfying grab/launch, a hijackable security vehicle, a legitimate escape path, and a Hall pedestal that records an episode with participants.

Test several play styles on the SAME content: all-stealth, noisy rescue, deliberate mayhem and solo creative obstacle bypass. The prototype is successful only if the player feels these are honest alternative expressions within one world.
